client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I keep trying to focus at work, but these memories of her just come out of nowhere and completely take over — I'll be in the middle of a task and suddenly I'm just... gone, thinking about her. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because no amount of conversation is going to bring her back.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — what you're experiencing, those waves of memory that pull you away, is a very natural and human response to grief, and it makes complete sense that you're struggling. You're absolutely right that nothing can bring her back, and I'd never want to suggest otherwise; but sometimes talking isn't about fixing the loss, it's about helping you carry it in a way that feels a little less overwhelming. I'm curious — when those memories come flooding in at work, what do you notice happening in your body or your thoughts in that moment?

client: When the memories hit, it's like my chest gets really tight and I kind of freeze up, like I can't think straight for a few minutes. Sometimes I'll be in the middle of a meeting or trying to focus on a report and suddenly I'm just... somewhere else entirely, back in her kitchen or something. And then I feel this guilt on top of it, like I should be holding it together better, like everyone around me is just waiting for me to get back to normal.
therapist: That tightness in your chest and the way you freeze — your body is doing something really important there, it's honoring a profound loss, and that's not a sign of weakness or falling apart. I also want to gently notice that thought — "I should be holding it together better" — because that sounds like a really harsh standard you're holding yourself to, and I wonder where that expectation is coming from. Who told you, or what made you believe, that there's a "normal" timeline for grieving someone you loved?

client: I guess... nobody told me directly, but watching my dad after my mom died, he just kept going. He went back to work after a week, he cooked dinner, he handled everything, and I remember thinking that's what strength looked like. So now I'm three months out from losing my best friend and I'm still crying in parking lots, and some part of me keeps comparing myself to this image of my dad and feeling like I'm failing some test I didn't even sign up for.
therapist: What a powerful insight — you've just uncovered where that "should" is coming from, and it's worth pausing on the fact that you built an entire definition of strength from watching one person, during one loss, from the outside, without ever really knowing what was happening inside him. It's also so telling that you call your grandmother your best friend, because that's not just a family loss — that's losing someone who was woven into your daily sense of self, and that kind of grief deserves so much more gentleness than you're giving yourself. I'm wondering — if a close friend came to you and said they were still crying in parking lots three months after losing their best friend, what would you actually say to them?

client: I'd probably tell them that's completely normal, that they're allowed to feel that way for as long as they need to. But when I try to apply that to myself it just... doesn't land the same way, like there's this wall that goes up and a voice that says "yeah but that's different, that's them, not you." I know logically what I'd say to a friend, but logic doesn't seem to touch whatever this thing is that keeps telling me I should be over it by now.
therapist: What you've just described — that gap between what you know and what you feel — is actually one of the most common and human experiences there is, and it doesn't mean you're broken or that this work isn't helping; it means the belief runs deeper than logic, closer to your identity. That voice that says "yeah but that's different" is worth getting curious about, because it's essentially arguing that you deserve less compassion than everyone else you love — and that's a pretty extraordinary claim. What do you think that voice is trying to protect you from, if you were to be as gentle with yourself as you'd be with a friend?

client: I've never really thought about it that way before — like the voice is actually trying to do something, protect me from something. I guess... maybe if I let myself off the hook, I'm afraid I'll just stop caring altogether, like the guilt is the only thing keeping me from being a truly terrible person. It's hard to imagine being gentle with myself without it feeling like I'm making excuses or just giving up on being better.
therapist: That's such a courageous and honest thing to recognize — that the guilt feels like proof of your love, like if you stop punishing yourself it means she mattered less, or that you're letting yourself get away with something. But I want to offer a gentle challenge to that: the fact that you're sitting here, still aching for her three months later, crying in parking lots, carrying her with you into every meeting — that *is* caring, deeply and completely, and it doesn't need guilt to keep it alive. What if gentleness with yourself wasn't the opposite of loving her, but actually another way of honoring the kind of person she saw when she looked at you?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me really wants to believe it. But it feels like... if I let myself off the hook, if I stop feeling this bad, then I'm just moving on, and moving on feels like betrayal. She always believed in me more than I believed in myself, and I'm not sure I deserve to be gentle with myself when I'm the one who's still here and she's not.
therapist: What you've just named — that surviving her feels like something you need to justify, like you owe it to her to suffer — that's such a tender and painful place to be, and it makes complete sense that it feels that way. But I want to sit with something you just said: she believed in you more than you believed in yourself, which means she already saw someone worthy of kindness and care — and I don't think the woman who held that belief in you would recognize "making yourself suffer" as the tribute you imagine it to be. If she could speak to you right now, in her kitchen, what do you think she would actually want for you?

client: I know what she would say. She'd probably tell me to stop being so hard on myself, to go eat something warm, to call a friend. But knowing that and actually believing I deserve it are two completely different things, and right now they feel miles apart.
therapist: That distance you're describing — between knowing and believing — that's not a flaw in you, that's actually the heart of the work, and the fact that you can so clearly hear her voice telling you to be gentle means some part of you is already holding onto what she wanted for you. We can't close that gap all at once, but I wonder if we don't have to — sometimes it starts with one small act, not because you fully believe you deserve it yet, but almost as an experiment, as a way of honoring her rather than yourself. What would it feel like to try just one of those things she'd suggest — the warm food, the call to a friend — not because you've earned it, but as a small act of love toward the person she believed in so deeply?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that framing would make it easier — doing it for her instead of for me. But honestly, when I think about actually picking up the phone and calling someone, I just imagine them hearing how hollow I sound and wondering what happened to me, and then I feel worse about myself, not better. I guess I'm scared that trying and having it feel empty will just confirm that I'm too far gone even for the things that used to help.
therapist: That fear — that trying and failing would be the final proof that you're beyond reach — that's such an important thing to name, because it's actually keeping you frozen in a place where the only way to stay safe is to never test it. But I want to gently point out that "hollow" and "too far gone" are your grief talking, not an objective truth about who you are, and the very fact that you can articulate this fear so clearly, that you're still reaching for something even in this conversation, suggests someone who is very much still here. I'm curious — when you imagine that phone call going badly, what specifically are you most afraid the other person would think or feel about you?

client: I guess what I'm most afraid of is that they'd feel burdened, like I'm this heavy thing they have to deal with after all this time of silence. Or worse, that they'd be polite about it, you know, kind of distant and careful with their words, and I'd be able to tell they were just trying to get off the phone. That would almost confirm everything I already believe about myself, that I pushed people away so thoroughly that even the ones who used to care have just moved on and I'm the only one still stuck here.
therapist: There's so much pain in that image — of reaching out and being met with polite distance — and I want to honor how real that fear feels, while also noticing that you've built a very detailed story about how that call would go before you've ever made it, and that story happens to perfectly confirm the harshest things you already believe about yourself. That's actually a really classic way our minds protect us from risk — by writing the ending in advance so we never have to find out — but it also means you've been living inside a story that may have very little to do with how the people who love you actually feel. I'm wondering — is there one person in your life, even just one, where if you're really honest with yourself, you're not completely sure they would respond with that polite distance?

client: I hate that you're right about that, because it makes me feel kind of stupid for not seeing it myself. There's my friend Dara — we've known each other since college, and she's never actually given me a reason to think she'd brush me off, but I still just... assume she would. I think I'm more scared that if I reach out and she's actually warm and present, then I have to face the fact that I've been isolating myself on purpose, and I don't know if I'm ready to sit with that.
therapist: You're not stupid at all — it takes real courage and clarity to see that, and what you just did is actually quite profound: you identified that the fear isn't really about Dara rejecting you, it's about what her warmth would ask of you, which is to take some responsibility for the walls you've built. That's a much scarier thing to face than rejection, because it means the isolation wasn't just something that happened to you — and sitting with that is genuinely hard work, not a character flaw. I'm curious — what do you think it would mean about you if it turned out you'd been choosing, even unconsciously, to keep people at a distance during the hardest months of your life?
